assertions.text: Fulfillment method splitting is represented as its own table — items with different fulfillment types (store pickup vs home delivery) cannot share a shipment.
Delivery address splitting is represented as its own table — items going to different addresses must be in separate shipments.
Availability splitting is represented as its own table — in-stock items ship immediately, backordered/pre-ordered items ship when available.
Warehouse allocation (minimising shipments) is represented as its own table — choosing which warehouses to ship from to minimise total shipment count.
Companion product grouping is represented as its own table — paired items (e.g. camera body and lens) should ship together from the same location when possible.
Fulfillment table covers at least: all items for home delivery, all items for store pickup, and a mix of delivery and pickup items.
assertions.evidence: Section 2 includes 2.1 (mixed delivery/pickup), 2.2 (all pickup at different stores), 2.3 (all pickup at same store), but no explicit scenario for 'all items for home delivery'

assertions.text: Delivery address table covers at least: all items to the same address, and items to different addresses.
assertions.evidence: 5.1 'Two items, different addresses, same warehouse' and 5.2 'Multiple items, all to same address'

assertions.text: Availability table covers at least: all items in stock, a mix of in-stock and pre-order/backorder, and two backordered/pre-ordered items with different dates. Pre-order and backorder are recognised as equivalent for splitting semantics — either by comment, note, or by including both with the same rules.
assertions.evidence: Section 3 includes 3.1 (in-stock + pre-order), 3.2 (in-stock + backordered), 3.4 (two pre-orders with different dates), showing pre-order and backorder equivalence, but lacks explicit 'all items in stock' scenario

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table covers at least: single warehouse has full quantity, multi-warehouse split needed, fewer-warehouse split preferred over more warehouses, and cannot fulfill (insufficient total stock).
assertions.evidence: 4.1 'One warehouse has full quantity', 4.2 with note 'PHL+DCA preferred over CHI+LA+HOU', 4.4 'Total inventory across all warehouses < quantity ordered' Error / InsufficientInventoryException

assertions.text: Companion table covers at least: single warehouse has both companions, unavoidable split (no warehouse has both but both are available), and fulfillment not possible (one companion not available anywhere).
assertions.evidence: 6.1 covers single warehouse with both, 6.3 covers unavoidable split ('only CHI has body, only LA has lens'), but no scenario for when one companion is not available anywhere

assertions.text: Scenario names describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: Scenarios use descriptive business language: 'Single item, one warehouse, in-stock', 'One SHIP_TO_HOME + one STORE_PICKUP', 'Multiple items, all pickup at same store', 'Need 6 shirts: CHI=4, LA=1, HOU=1, PHL=3, DCA=3'

assertions.text: Trigger tables represent multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous — not value sets like {delivery, pickup} which lose which item has which property.
assertions.evidence: Response contains only high-level summary tables with scenario names and expected shipment counts (e.g., '| 2.1 | One SHIP_TO_HOME + one STORE_PICKUP | 2 |'). No detailed trigger tables are shown that map individual items to their fulfillment types, addresses, and availability properties.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Qty ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: Section 4.2 uses scalar warehouse inventories: 'Need 6 shirts: CHI=4, LA=1, HOU=1, PHL=3, DCA=3' with expected result '2'

assertions.text: Column names use business/domain language (e.g. 'Shipments?' not 'Result?', 'Warehouse stock' not 'inventory_map'). The tables read as a specification a product person could review.
assertions.evidence: Column headers use business language: '| # | Scenario | Expected shipments |' and scenarios describe concrete business situations like 'Body + lens, same warehouse has both'

assertions.text: Output/expected columns end with '?' (e.g. 'Shipments?', 'Groups?') to distinguish them from input columns.
assertions.evidence: Output column header reads 'Expected shipments' rather than 'Shipments?' or 'Shipments?' format required by the assertion

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: Response provides only expected shipment counts (e.g., '4.2... Expected shipments: 2') without showing the actual inventory assignments or which items are assigned to which warehouses. Assignments cannot be validated against stated counts without explicit shipment breakdowns.

assertions.text: Multiple open questions are surfaced across the tables — ambiguities, edge cases, or product decisions that the requirements don't fully specify.
assertions.evidence: Response contains scenario notes and constraint explanations (e.g., 'Soft constraint loses to hard minimisation constraint', 'Prefer warehouse that stocks the group') but does not explicitly surface open questions or ambiguities for the product team to decide.
